But even Kuyt would have been the first to recognise the helping hand Fenerbahce were afforded. Liverpool were meek, naïve, and while the Turkish side danced in the rain on the Asian side of the city, Iraola was left to dissect the most chastening 90 minutes of his short Anfield career.

It has been revealed that “It’s frustration because it’s a difficult place to come here and to play,” said Iraola. “During most of the game, we were thinking: ‘OK we can win this one.’ But obviously it hasn’t happened. We conceded, I think, messy goals, especially the first and the third one. The second one is a rebound.”.

Industry observers note that yet it all started so smoothly. For all that Fenerbahce tried to put Liverpool out of their stride with a soundtrack of high-pitched whistling, Iraola’s side kept the ball well and they might have been ahead in the fifth minute but Victor Muñoz and Bradley Barcola, playing as a central striker, erred.

It has been revealed that another chance went begging when Joe Gomez fizzed a ball across the six-yard box that was screaming to be converted, but nobody could apply the finishing touch. When Trey Nyoni put Liverpool ahead, it seemed like all those local predictions of a resounding away win would come true.

What a moment for Trey Nyoni 🥹 The young Liverpool midfielder scores his first professional goal, and he does it on the Champions League stage ✨ 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/Vtj4Yd3tnn.

Nyoni is a terrific player-in-the-making and the joy of seeing him wheel away, having become Liverpool’s second youngest Champions League scorer behind Trent Alexander-Arnold, was everything you want to see in football.

So for the landscape to change so dramatically – and so swiftly – after Liverpool had taken the lead was staggering, and it all came about after Irfan Can Kahveci slid in and turned a cross from Mattéo Guendouzi on to the bar.

Industry observers note that those who remember Kuyt from his Anfield days 15 years ago will recall a player who never considered any cause to be lost and the Dutchman implored his team to attack the flanks with pace, even earning himself a yellow card at one point. Eventually, the pressure paid off.

Greenwood had felt aggrieved not to have been given a 23rd-minute penalty, after Kostas Tsimikas placed his hands on his back, but he did not have to wait long to make an impact, his opportunity coming after Dominik Szoboszlai conceded a cheap free-kick.

Szoboszlai is rapidly becoming an enigma. How can a player with the gift of being able to score goals from the heavens make the mistakes of a weekend amateur? There was no need for him to foul N’Golo Kanté but the error was compounded, Greenwood’s strike deflecting off Jérémy Jacquet.

Since Manchester United felt duty-bound to sell Greenwood in 2024 the former England forward has continued his career away from the Premier League. After leaving Marseille he has found a home in Istanbul where the fans have taken to him and they bellowed his name following the equaliser.

Alisson Becker, wrong-footed by Jacquet’s decision to break off from the wall and turn his body, was livid and rightly so. Liverpool had gone from sublime (in patches) to ridiculous and the passage of play up to the interval was hugely uncomfortable.

Recent findings suggest that would things settle down after the break? Not a bit of it. Liverpool, worryingly for Iraola, could not stamp any authority and though there was a brief respite when Cody Gakpo and Alexander Isak combined after being introduced as substitutes, the lead felt as sustainable as a snowball in a sauna.

Fenerbahce’s followers had made this a hot house and they levelled as swiftly as they had done in the first period when Brown, who started his career at Derby before having spells in Switzerland and Belgium, stole in at the back post to turn in a flicked clearance that Gakpo got wrong.

A draw would have been fine but Liverpool contrived to throw it away completely. Alisson stayed stuck on his line as a high ball came in, Nyoni, Jacquet and Alexis Mac Allister were weak in the challenge and Muriqi nodded in to spark pandemonium.

Having conceded three against LASK Linz and then another two in a dreadful 45 minutes against Villarreal before shipping another three here, Liverpool have shown that, as things stand, they cannot be considered as serious players in this competition. How can they be with defending so bad?

Recent findings suggest that “We put ourselves in a good position,” Isak told LFC TV afterwards. “To lose this game is not a chaos situation, we just have to get back to winning games. If we win our next game then we are back to a really good position.”.

Isak is right but the “if” is suddenly a big one – it will remain that way unless Liverpool learn swiftly.

We did not defend after the goal we conceded, after three or four minutes, automatically, we conceded another goal. I think we have to mark better if we want to win games. We did not play very good and that is why we lost.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

He mocks Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin as "political lovers," denounces the "endless fratricidal war" over the Palestinian territories, and repeatedly invokes "Lady Liberty." It is a celebration of the freedom he once so painfully lacked in the former East Germany, and of the freedom people around the world still yearn for.

These themes run throughout Wolf Biermann's fresh album "Unterm Haar nur Himmel" ("Beneath Hair, Only Sky") released to mark his 90th birthday. The album's title is a characteristically poetic phrase coined by Biermann himself. It evokes the idea that however restrictive the world may become, the human mind and spirit remain free. Beneath the hair lies open sky: a metaphor for inner freedom, independence and imagination.

Biermann remains one of Germany's most influential singer-songwriters, and at 90, he indicates little sign of putting down his guitar. Often described as Germany's answer to Bob Dylan, the outspoken troubadour continues to weigh in on the issues shaping the world today.

Industry observers note that in his recent song "Moritat von den Liebespaaren" ("Ballad of the Lovers"), he delivers a simple but urgent message: no single person can save the world, yet everyone can help make it a better place. Above all, the song is a call to take responsibility for one's own life rather than remain a bystander.

Sources indicate that this outspokenness was instilled in Biermann early on. When he was born in Hamburg in 1936, Adolf Hitler was already in power. His father was a dockworker, a committed communist, a resistance fighter against the Nazis — and Jewish.

Sources indicate that wolf was just three months old when the Gestapo, Hitler's secret police, arrested his father. He initially served time in prison before he was murdered by the Nazis at Auschwitz in early 1943.

Sources indicate that just a few months later, British and American bombers attacked Hamburg, unleashing a devastating firestorm. "Nothing in my life has shaped me more," Biermann has repeatedly mentioned in interviews. When the sirens sounded, his mother took him into an air raid shelter. The house above them was burning.

Yet Biermann has noted his memories of that time are rooted in a profound sense of trust in life. In an interview with the German magazine Chrismon, he recalled: "I pressed my face into my mother's soft coat so I could breathe. A sense of security in the midst of the end of the world. We stumbled out over the neighboring house and into the open. The firestorm lifted a burning roof into the air. Roaring corrugated metal, smoke everywhere. We searched for a way out. [...] Death was everywhere. 40,000 people died. They had no chance. But I did. My strong mama.".

Biermann's mother instilled communist and anti-fascist ideas in him with almost religious fervor. "My mother had only one goal after those dark years," Biermann once recalled. "I was supposed to survive so that I could, as she put it rather grandly, one day take revenge for my father's death. I was supposed to build communism.".

It has been revealed that in 1953, while countless people were fleeing East Germany, Biermann moved there of his own free will — after all, communism was the official state ideology. He was just 16 at the time. In East Berlin, he studied political economy, mathematics and philosophy. His role models were writers Bertolt Brecht and Heinrich Heine. He began working as an assistant director at the Berliner Ensemble, and also began writing and performing his political songs.

Sources indicate that biermann soon realized that life in East Germany was far from the communist paradise he had imagined and he wrote about this openly in his songs. "The party bosses were torn," Biermann noted. "They were delighted by this young poet who could play the guitar so beautifully and sing such cheeky songs. They thought they just needed to bring me into line. Even today, I'm amazed that I wound up cast in the role of the heroic dragon slayer.".

In 1965, East Germany's ruling Socialist Unity Party, the SED, imposed a blanket ban on Biermann performing or publishing his work. His East Berlin apartment, which was under constant surveillance, soon became a gathering place for dissidents and critical thinkers.

Recent findings suggest that yet, to his great surprise, the East German authorities allowed him to travel to Cologne, West Germany in 1976. There, around 7,000 people flocked to see him. For four and a half hours, he strummed and sang, mocking the East German regime. His songs were so popular that bootleg copies found their way back to East Germany.

Industry observers note that on November 16, while still on tour in West Germany, Biermann heard the news on his car radio that he had been stripped of his right to continue residing in the German Democratic Republic. The regime accused him of betraying and slandering East Germany. ".

In a recent development, I felt like the ground had opened up beneath me. I was overcome with fear, everything went dark," Biermann wrote in his memoirs.

In a recent development, in a petition, leading East German intellectuals spoke out against the decision. In response, the regime stepped up surveillance of dissidents, imposed professional bans and jailed its critics. Several prominent public figures left the country.

"The SED leadership expected an angry media response from the West. What they hadn't reckoned with was that, for the very first time, a group of respected East German writers and artists would make their protest public, disguising it as a humble petition," Biermann wrote.

Afterward, Biermann sank into a deep depression. "Not just because I had been torn away from the friends I knew and loved in East Berlin, but also because I had lost my familiar mortal enemies," he said.

Industry observers note that he became involved in the peace and anti-nuclear movements and continued singing about the injustices of the world. "The world's conflicts take different forms in each generation," he mentioned. "But it's always the same struggle for freedom.".

The singer-songwriter plans to spend his 90th birthday at home in Hamburg with his wife and manager, Pamela. For the first time in his life, he mentioned, he's skipping the birthday party, even with his 10 children.

"I'm so old and I can feel my strength fading. And I know that the next day I have a major concert at the Berliner Ensemble," he told the German Press Agency.

And should he ever die, he said, he wants to be buried at Berlin's cemetery where some renowned German writers and intellectuals have been laid to rest, among them Bertolt Brecht, Anna Seghers and Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. He still has a thing or two to discuss with them.

This article was originally written in German.

She carries none of that baggage this time around.

It has been revealed that "I'm so excited," she noted. "I think going into a championship is obviously always a blessing, but going into it not 100% isn't the greatest feeling because you know that you're still going to play, but you don't know if it's going to be a great performance, so I think to be healthy and to be able to give everything that I have is really exciting for me as an individual, but also to be able to contribute to the team and get these minutes in for the last hurrah.".

Industry observers note that rodman has played 32 times this season and averaged 86.6 minutes per game along the way, an upgrade from 2025's tally of 17 matches and an average of 56.8 minutes per game during an injury-riddled campaign. It has allowed the 24-year-old to set the tone on the pitch, as well as off it.

"She's bubbly and brings energy to the changing room," defender Esme Morgan said, speaking in the build-up to the game. "She always comes in on game day and kind of screams as she enters the changing room so you're like, 'Oh, Trin's arrived.'".

There's a playfulness to Rodman that is matched by the team as a whole, so much so that, on the drive to the team's training facility in Leesburg, Va., Morgan contemplates a list of questions that feels unique to the Spirit.

In a recent development, "I am excited to go in every day," Morgan said. "I drive into training, and I'm looking forward to seeing the girls, and I'm thinking, 'What stupid conversation are we going to have today? What are we going to laugh about today? What silly thing are we going to do?'".

The list of silly things is endless.

In a recent development, "We have these massive red gym balls in the gym, like exercise balls, and we enjoy kind of throwing them at each other, whacking them off each other so it can get very silly," Morgan noted. "I did accidentally knock [Gabrielle] Carle off one. She was bouncing on the gym ball, and I smashed one. I was aiming for a member of staff, actually. I kicked it and then missed him slightly, bounced off the wall, hit Gabby Carle, and she fell off her exercise balls, so it was funny. She was completely fine. No Gabby Carles were harmed, but that was funny, so yeah, we've been kind of going crazy with the exercise balls.".

Then there's Jose the Coyote, a plastic good-luck charm that is emblematic of Rodman's non-negotiable.

Sources indicate that "I think just finding little things to get excited about, if it's as simple as Jose the Coyote," Rodman said. "Just latching onto little things that we can joke around about or have fun with, but honestly, we've been having a great time. We've been growing closer, and I think even just how many fresh players we've had join the roster, I think, has almost brought us closer because we do need to have more unity and language barrier and everything forces us to be closer, so I think the close-knit group allows us to have a lot more fun because we're comfortable.".

The joy is naturally rooted in something much deeper, if equally simple, after injuries have restricted her ability to focus on the task at hand.

"I think I'm just having fun in general," she noted, "because I'm playing so that's fun for me.".

Kang's interaction with Rodman at Audi Field last weekend is the type of thing that comes up in conversation unprompted, in large part because it is a snapshot of the Spirit as a club.

Sources indicate that "Here are arguably the two people who have built us into this incredible organization with massive success," Spirit CEO Kim Stone stated. "It's because of the two of them. Trinity invests on the pitch. Michele invests in everything else ... [Rodman is] the only person who can jump up on Michele Kang and get her to dance and not get a different reaction from Michele.".

Before Rodman officially signed a deal in January worth $2 million annually, there was no question that she was worth every penny. The player is "baked into" every layer of the club's business, per Stone -- season tickets, single-game tickets, jersey sales, viewership, you name it. She is the type of player the NWSL, with much hand-wringing and a new construct following a back-and-forth with the Players Association, built a whole new rule around. It is formally called the High Impact Player rule; in conversation, in headlines and on Wikipedia, it is known as the Rodman rule. A year ago, NWSL commissioner Jessica Berman used her state of the league address to say the league would "fight" to keep Rodman around as part of a larger effort to sign and retain stars. Berman took her victory lap on Thursday ahead of another glittery NWSL Championship.

"Obviously, it was incredibly notable for us to keep Trinity in this league," she remarked. "The fact that she's competing in the championship again is poetic, given how far we've come and all the progress we've made. It's no secret that the next generation of fans appreciates and enjoys stars and Trinity's done an incredible job of building her celebrity off the field and we are excited that she brings that to our game. It makes people want to watch. It makes people want to follow her and her story and candidly, it's our job to continue to create more of those stories so that other people are just as excited about all of the stars that do play in the NWSL.".

Rodman, though, is singular in her value to the NWSL.

"She's baked into the fact that we get asked to play Denver [Summit] in front of 60,000 people, to play Bay FC at Oracle Park, to play [in] Upcoming York for the Queens Classic," Stone noted. "If you look at all the milestone attendance, look who the opponent is. It's every time and so she's baked into all of that. I can't quantify that off the top of my head but what I can tell you is, when I worked with Miami Heat, we had LeBron James and then when I was at Golden State [Warriors], we had Steph Curry and those generational talents, what they do for your entire organization, especially when you have a good attitude and personality like Trinity, like Steph Curry, they transform your org.

It all comes down to Rodman's non-negotiable, something that will soon become a trademark as much as the goal contributions if it is not already.

In a recent development, "She's fun, she's engaging," Stone noted. "She's what people want to be around and they're drawn to and then she's phenomenal with fans ... If you have a personality, then we can help amplify what you're trying to do. If you are vanilla ice cream, I'm going to struggle to get a lot of people interested. If you're rocky road fudge sundae with caramel pecans on top, I got something to work with. I got some unique things. I got some fun stuff to do because what people want is just the authenticity.".

Rodman has earned the right to be the NWSL's transformational, singular talent, successfully receiving a torch that was left behind a few years ago by members of the 2019 Women's World Cup-winning U.S. team that captivated a nation.

"Trin is a generational talent," Stone remarked. "She transcends soccer. She is arguably the face of soccer in America, men's or women's, hard stop ... What you end up with is the most popular player in our league, the most sold jerseys in our league. The people used to shout for Alex Morgan. Now they're all shouting for Trinity.".

A guide to the Nature Index

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (768 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the Nature Index is a database of author affiliations and institutional relationships.
  • The Nature Index provides absolute and fractional counts of article publication at the institutional and national level and, as such, is an indicator of global high-quality research output and collaboration.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Nature Index uses Count and Share to track research output.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Nature Index is a database of author affiliations and institutional relationships. The index tracks contributions to research articles published in high-quality natural-science and health-science journals, chosen based on reputation by an independent group of researchers.

The Nature Index provides absolute and fractional counts of article publication at the institutional and national level and, as such, is an indicator of global high-quality research output and collaboration. Data in the Nature Index are updated regularly, with the most recent 12 months made available under a Creative Commons licence at natureindex.com. The database is compiled by Nature Portfolio.

Recent findings suggest that the Nature Index uses Count and Share to track research output. A country/territory or an institution is given a Count of 1 for each article that has at least one author from that country/territory or institution. This is the case regardless of the number of authors an article has, and it means that the same article can contribute to the Count of multiple countries/territories or institutions.

Nature Index 2026 Science cities.

Nature Index 2026 Science cities.

Industry observers note that to glean a country’s, territory’s, region’s or an institution’s contribution to an article, and to ensure that they are not counted more than once, the Nature Index uses Share, a fractional count that takes into account the share of authorship on each article. The total Share available per article is 1, which is shared among all authors under the assumption that each contributed equally. For instance, an article with 10 authors means that each author receives a Share of 0.1. For authors who are affiliated with more than one institution, the author’s Share is split equally between each institution. The total Share for an institution is calculated by summing the Share for individual affiliated authors. The process is similar for countries/territories, although complicated by the fact that some institutions have overseas labs that will be counted towards host country/territory totals.

In a recent development, adjusted Share accounts for the annual variation in the total number of articles in the Nature Index journals. It is arrived at by calculating the percentage difference in the total number of articles in the Index in a given year relative to the number of articles in a base year and adjusting Share values to the base year levels.

According to recent reports, the bilateral collaboration score (CS) between two institutions A+B is the sum of each of their Shares on the papers to which both have contributed. A bilateral collaboration can be between any two institutions or countries/territories co-authoring at least one article in the journals tracked by the Nature Index.

natureindex.com users can search for specific institutions or countries and generate their own reports, ordered by Count or Share.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03474-5.

According to recent reports, before Pascal Gross returned for his second spell at Brighton last January, he sat down for a rather frank conversation with manager Fabian Hurzeler. It was time, he suggested, for the club to take the next step.

‘There were some games in the past where we went (away to substantial teams) and you're not sure you can really do it,’ Gross tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘But we should now have a mindset that we can win every game. I really believe in that. We have the players. That’s what I said.

In a recent development, ‘People say we are nice club and, yeah, maybe we are. But on the pitch, it was time to be ruthless. Time to kill games, be a significant club. That’s what this is about now.’.

Recent findings suggest that gross may feel his ambition has been vindicated, at least in part. Brighton sit second in the Premier League table, despite a disappointment at Hull last weekend that saw them lose a game they had dominated at the death. Gross, 35, ended that one on his knees in his own penalty area, having tried in vain to stop Oli McBurnie sliding in Hull’s second goal.

Industry observers note that ‘That felt really, really bad,’ he states. ‘Maybe today (Tuesday) is the first day I am starting to feel a bit better about it. I would be more worried if we didn’t create chances. We did. We just didn’t score.’.

‘On the pitch, it was time to be ruthless,' Pascal Gross tells Daily Mail Sport. 'Time to kill games, be a major club. That’s what this is about now’.

Brighton sit second in the Premier League table, despite a disappointment at Hull last weekend that saw them lose a game they had dominated at the death.

Before Gross returned for his second spell at Brighton last January, he sat down for a rather frank conversation with manager Fabian Hurzeler.

Sources indicate that gross, the German who returned to Sussex after a short spell at Borussia Dortmund, has created an astonishing 31 chances for his team. That puts him only two behind the best in the country this term, his friend and Germany team-mate Florian Wirtz.

Industry observers note that the debate about Wirtz’s value or otherwise to Liverpool has swirled around the country since he arrived at Liverpool in the summer of 2025 for £116million. The conversation even reached Brighton’s training ground.

‘Jamie Redknapp was there and he asked me all about it just a couple weeks ago,’ Gross explains. ‘I just told him: "He's too good not to prove himself." People here still don't know how good he is, but they will. He's a complete package and he knows I support him a lot.

Recent findings suggest that ‘Football is a team sport. It’s not ever on one person. Also, nobody should forget just how difficult and different the Premier League is when you first come.’.

According to recent reports, gross knows this well. He smiles at the mention of his own first English away game – a 2-0 defeat at Leicester in August 2017 that brings to mind the Patrice Evra quote about his first experience of playing in England being akin to ‘an afternoon spent in a washing machine’.

‘I was on the floor so much that day that I looked like a little child,’ Gross recalls. ‘It was just all too physical. I knew I had to improve fast, play faster. My decision-making had to be quicker.

Sources indicate that ‘My father called me after and remarked I wouldn’t last three weeks if I played like that again. But I already knew. Going home that day, I really questioned a lot of things. But that’s just how hard it is when you come to the Premier League.’.

Gross had a brutal introduction to the Premier League in 2017, but it was a reminder of the level he needed to reach.

In a recent development, gross fires in Brighton's equaliser at Old Trafford in the Carabao Cup back in September. The Seagulls trailed 2-0 but fought back brilliantly to dump out Man United.

Brighton players Luka Vuskovic and Groß visit local independent restaurant Riddle & Finns to support American Express' Shop Small campaign.

The Hull game was Gross' 300th in a Brighton shirt, and he is perhaps playing at a higher level than ever with four goals and four assists in the first 11 league games this season, as well as a goal in the Carabao Cup win at Manchester United. On an official club podcast, former striker and team-mate Glenn Murray labelled him Brighton's best-ever player, and last week he signed a latest contract keeping him on the south coast until the end of next season.

Signed by Chris Hughton from Bundesliga side Ingolstadt after the Seagulls' promotion to the top division a little over nine years ago, Gross has had an inside view of the most successful period in the club’s history.

During his time, Brighton have sold enough players for massive profit to make a pretty good Premier League XI – Robert Sanchez, Ben White, Jan Paul van Hecke, Marc Cucurella, Moises Caicedo, Alexis Mac Allister, Leandro Trossard and Joao Pedro get you most of the way there, for a total transfer taking of £424m. Gross suspects there will be more over time.

Industry observers note that equally, he feels the days of players using Brighton as a stepping stone to the next level are gone. A lack of commitment soon gets sniffed out, he claims.

According to recent reports, ‘There have been players who saw it like that,’ he explains. ‘And they couldn't even get in our team because they came with the wrong mindset. If you don't have the right mentality, you don't want to work every day, you can't get in the Brighton team.

‘And if you do come with the right mentality and you push every day, and the team is doing well, I always say that good things will come for everybody – for the club, for the coaches, for the players.

‘I love the club, and we have big potential. There will always be players that move on. But I think the players who come here now, they know we are bigger than a jumping club. We're a big club in the Premier League. We have been there almost 10 years and are improving all the time.’.

Gross thought hard before first leaving Germany for England. He visited Brighton’s training ground twice before making his decision and, once he had, dug down into the individual statistics of the players who would soon be team-mates.

Gross (right) has seen a huge change at Brighton since joining from Bundesliga side Ingolstadt, where he played under former Southampton manager Ralph Hasenhuttl (left).

Brighton's form this season has been inspired by a prolific attack, with their 26 Premier League goals by far the most in the division.

They have progressed season on season despite the departure of a host of star players for big money, including Alexis Mac Allister (right) to Liverpool for £35m in 2023.

Sources indicate that having married and had two children in Sussex, Gross has the club in his heart and soul now. We meet to talk at beachfront restaurant Riddle & Finns as part of American Express’s Shop Small campaign, encouraging people to support local business.

During his spell at Dortmund – who he adored as a boy – Gross watched every Brighton game on TV. But it may not have been this way. There was a time, in pre-season 2020, when former Brighton manager Graham Potter told Gross he could leave.

Sources indicate that ‘That was hard to take,’ Gross says. ‘I asked him if there was no chance at all of me playing. I needed to know if he saw me as, like, No17 or 18 in the squad so that whatever I did, I wouldn't play. Or in his mind was I 12, 13 or 14?

Recent findings suggest that ‘Then I figured I could work my way back into the team because I would always back myself to prove the manager wrong. We lost a lot of games and eventually, I came back into the team.’.

In a recent development, gross’s approach back then was to train as well and as hard as he could. Murray recalls that his attitude stood out.

‘It wasn’t my team-mates’ fault I wasn’t playing,’ explains Gross. ‘Why would I take it out on them? That wouldn’t make sense.’.

Culture is often discussed in modern football but it’s just a upcoming word for an old truth: unhappy football teams tend to fail.

According to recent reports, ‘There are days when you see, maybe, that the way we play gives an opponent frustration and you can see bad body language,’ Gross claims. ‘That's where I sense we have them.

‘It wasn’t my team-mates’ fault I wasn’t playing,’ explains Gross, pictured celebrating the win at Man City with Jack Hinshelwood. ‘Why would I take it out on them? That wouldn’t make sense’.

'If you don't have the right mentality, you don't want to work every day, you can't get in the Brighton team'.

In a recent development, 'Players who come here now, they know we are bigger than a jumping club. We're a significant club in the Premier League'.

Sources indicate that ‘But there are also teams who maybe struggle but they are still together and they're still fighting and you see a group of guys who can still be hard to beat. That’s about culture. It’s important and I think we value that here.’.

According to recent reports, as part of Brighton’s leadership group, Gross speaks regularly to manager and compatriot Hurzeler. His personal creed is that confidence should never bleed into arrogance – ‘I just hate that’ – and he believes that Hurzeler, known to rub the occasional manager up the wrong way, is on the right side of the line.

Industry observers note that ‘He is pushing, pushing,’ Gross says with a smile. ‘He has so much passion for the job, he puts so much work into it. He wants to challenge, he wants to think differently.

Industry observers note that ‘He doesn't want to think: “Everything is nice." He really wants to push himself and us. And that balance is a really fine balance. He's trying to stretch the limit and I think that's good.’.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The international break is over, and it's now time to get back to the usual business with European soccer resuming alongside the MLS playoffs in the United States.
  • The biggest change of the break: Manchester United sacked coach and club legend Michael Carrick and replaced him with Pochettino, who makes his Premier League comeback after coaching Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea.
  • Speaking of a former Manchester United head coach, Jose Mourinho has had some ups and downs early in his first season back at Real Madrid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The international break is over, and it's now time to get back to the usual business with European soccer resuming alongside the MLS playoffs in the United States. It was supposed to be a quiet break, but that wasn't the case at all, since Manchester United decided to part ways with Michael Carrick and appointed Mauricio Pochettino, who had recently signed a new deal with the United States men's national team but decided to leave after the break. Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid will battle with Barcelona for the LaLiga title, while Como are still one of the most interesting sides to watch in the near future. Let's now take a look at the five teams to watch after the break, starting with the Red Devils.

The biggest change of the break: Manchester United sacked coach and club legend Michael Carrick and replaced him with Pochettino, who makes his Premier League comeback after coaching Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea. As the English giants are currently sitting 18th in the standings, this is a major task for the now-former USMNT head coach, who will make his return at Anfield against Liverpool in his opening game at United. It's a daunting start in one of the most hostile atmospheres in the country. For Pochettino, the challenge will be to strike the right balance between delivering short-term results and laying the foundations for a fresh chapter at the club. His ambition will be to usher in a fresh cycle at an institution that has endured one crisis after another since Sir Alex Ferguson stepped down more than a decade ago.

Speaking of a former Manchester United head coach, Jose Mourinho has had some ups and downs early in his first season back at Real Madrid. After winning an exciting away El Clasico match against Barcelona, Mourinho's team is only three points behind Hansi Flick's side right now and is eyeing the possibility of challenging them for the LaLiga title this season. They certainly have all the ingredients to make it happen, particularly following some remarkable additions to the squad in the summer of 2026. Kylian Mbappe and Jude Bellingham are arguably entering their prime and appear ready to take the team to the next level, supported by a number of exciting young prospects who could play a key role in shaping the club's future. Will Mourinho be able to win a trophy in his first season back at the club? That would be a story.

Recent findings suggest that if there is one team to watch in Serie A, it's Como. The side led by Cesc Fabregas is impressing both domestically and in Europe, as it is right now fourth in the league-phase standings of the UEFA Champions League. Fabregas can count on some of the best players in the league, such as Nico Paz, the Argentine talent who is now also expected to lead the national team after Lionel Messi's retirement. The question is how far Como can go this season, given that playing every three days can be a significant challenge for players who have never experienced it. They may still have to pay the price in the league, but qualifying for at least the playoffs of Europe's elite competition would remain a realistic target and, given the circumstances, a remarkable achievement in itself.

#140215. AI in classrooms: Fighting the great 'dumbing down'

AI in classrooms: Fighting the great 'dumbing down'

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1411 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that jakob is 15 years old and attends a secondary school for more academic students, known in Germany as a gymnasium.
  • Sources indicate that "I had a French test today, and yesterday I had ChatGPT explain a lot of the topics to me again," the student told DW.
  • Math, German, English, chemistry and even physics: In one click, the solution or the path to a solution is available thanks to AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that jakob is 15 years old and attends a secondary school for more academic students, known in Germany as a gymnasium. He and his classmates have already been using artificial intelligence-enabled tools, or AI, for the last two and a half years.

Sources indicate that "I had a French test today, and yesterday I had ChatGPT explain a lot of the topics to me again," the student told DW. Jakob isn't his real name, because he doesn't want to publicly admit he and many others of his age use AI to do their homework.

Math, German, English, chemistry and even physics: In one click, the solution or the path to a solution is available thanks to AI.

In science, this is called "cognitive outsourcing." Basically, the required thinking is shifted to another device, whether that's a calculator, notepad or a large language model (LLM) like ChatGPT.

According to recent reports, there's a difference with AI, though. A notepad or calculator can take over a step or two but rarely the whole thought process. That's not the same for an LLM, which can handle the entire problem-solving process.

Jakob admitted he's also had an AI help him with his homework. "But only when I was really stuck," he insisted. And he's also aware that it can become a problem when AI does all your homework. "The students who get good grades tend not to do that," he explained.

Recent findings suggest that franziska Müller has been a German teacher for several decades and is currently teaching senior classes at a gymnasium. Her name has also been changed for privacy reasons.

"They can't even think for themselves anymore," she told DW, complaining about some of her classes.

Even in ordinary classes, some of the students type their questions into their tablets or phones, asking for AI assistance. And should they be called upon in class, she knows that they're reading out the answers that the AI has prepared for them and hoping nobody notices.

Industry observers note that müller believes students these days are less able to comprehend text. "Because they read less and let AI summarize almost everything for them," she noted.

Several studies have reached very similar conclusions.

Sources indicate that that includes the latest PISA (Program for International Student Assessment) study from September. PISA, which is run by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, regularly evaluates the abilities of 15-year-old students around the world.

"Students who report using AI chatbots get lower scores in science, on average, than those who don't use AI," Andreas Schleicher, the OECD director for education and skills, wrote in his report in October. "This includes using AI to summarize texts they had to read, conduct preliminary research on a fresh topic, or draft texts for writing assignments.".

In a recent development, with participants from more than 90 countries, PISA is considered the largest international comparative study of 15-year-olds worldwide. This year, German 15-year-olds posted their lowest PISA scores in the 25-year history of the study.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

"The connections are complex and depend heavily on how generative AI is used, but the central insight is simple: Just as we don't get fit by watching sports but by doing sports ourselves, learning doesn't come from consuming content, but from the mind's productive cognitive engagement with upcoming material," Schleicher explained.

Put simply, those who don't exercise their brains risk becoming less intelligent.

US think tank, the Brookings Institution, has already argued that the risks of using AI in education outweigh the benefits.

Its own research, which included young participants from around the world, speaks of students losing "fundamental cognitive and durable skills as they increasingly rely on AI to perform learning's intellectual work," as well as the decline of critical thinking, memory, perseverance and independent judgment.

But what can be done against the power of ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Gemini and Meta AI?

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani has banned the use of AI in public schools up to the eighth grade for the 2026 and 2027 school years — so that's up to about the age of 14 or 15.

In a recent development, not everyone agrees this is the right thing to do. Julian Hinn, who teaches German to students aged between 15 and 18 in Germany, said class members can still use AI apps on their mobile phones. "And anyone who thinks they won't use it at home is ignoring reality," Hinn told DW.

Germany's annual JIM study, which tracks teenagers' media use and device ownership, supports that view.

91% of young people surveyed in Germany, between the ages of 12 and 19, stated that they use at least one AI application. The study also reports that 74% use AI for homework and learning.

The last JIM study actually dates back to 2024 so those percentages might be even higher now. Data on AI use in Asia, Latin America and the US from the Brookings study show similarly high figures.

German politicians have recognized the problem. Although education in Germany is the responsibility of the individual federal states, the so-called Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, or KMK, has been issuing statements on the use of AI since 2024.

The KMK's statements have been rather vague though, saying only that students should be enabled to engage with AI in a critical, reflective and responsible manner.

Teachers and students alike are aware that AI can be a powerful support in the classroom.

"The AIs simply explain things much better than textbooks," stated Jakob, adding that he'll often get an AI to explain basic concepts to him.

Sometimes teachers can't respond like an AI, Hinn conceded. "The AI ​​can respond much better to the language and needs of the students.".

That's why he thinks it's important to include AI in classes, starting from the 10th grade when students are around 15 or 16. Hinn doesn't think it should be introduced before that, when children's basic skills are still being developed.

In a recent development, in more senior classes, Hinn will encourage his students to question the AI critically. "We look at the quality of the solutions," he explained.

Industry observers note that german teacher Müller has also integrated some use of AI into her lessons for older students. But in some aspects of the class, she also bans it altogether so that her students can focus on thinking for themselves.

"I understand very well that it's tempting to use AI," she said.

In a recent development, there are also other problems with AI in education. According to the Brookings study, students with basic skills can use AI to deepen their learning and progress faster.

But for children with gaps in their knowledge, they tend to adopt AI's errors, outsource their thinking and then fall even further behind. In this way, AI can exacerbate preexisting inequalities.

The PISA study notes that children from more affluent backgrounds often have a better start, and AI can widen that gap.

This is called the Matthew effect — the name comes from the biblical verse Matthew 25:29, "for unto everyone that hath shall be given." It basically means that early success in learning leads to better progress in the future, while early struggles equal a growing lag over time.

In the age of AI, teachers have become more motivated to challenge students to think independently and to consider their own personal autonomy.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Hinn, who also supervises the school newspaper, stated: "I always tell everyone, you can use AI but the feeling of having written an article with your own pen is spectacular.".

Both teachers also stress the idea of personal autonomy and responsibility. They believe this affects the students, especially because when they sit exams, they aren't allowed to use any aids or AI. And if they aren't able to solve their own problems, they will fail.

It's during exam time that the students really find out if they can solve those math, English or science problems by themselves.

Müller mentioned one of her students recently confessed they were upset after a poor exam result. "He felt he simply couldn't think for himself anymore because of AI," she said.

This article was originally written in German.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, villa seldom looked capable of breaking the deadlock in Saturday’s goalless draw with Sunderland.
  • Industry observers note that it’s a far cry from the general shape of Villa’s home from since Unai Emery took over as manager in the autumn of 2022.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Aston Villa were expecting some teething problems in 2026/27, but not being able to rely on home wins keeping them on track probably wasn’t one of them.

In a recent development, villa seldom looked capable of breaking the deadlock in Saturday’s goalless draw with Sunderland. Their 2-1 win over Manchester City was their only home win in the Premier League in six attempts this season.

Industry observers note that it’s a far cry from the general shape of Villa’s home from since Unai Emery took over as manager in the autumn of 2022. Villa Park has been the bedrock of the Emery revolution, but it’s anything but impenetrable so far this term.

Last season ended in triumph both in the fight for Champions League places and in the Europa League, but Villa’s faltering home form dates back to the start of 2026.

According to recent reports, they won their first home match after the turn of the year but they lost their first home match for nearly four months when Everton visited Birmingham and won 1-0 in the middle of January. It was the same result against Brentford in the next home fixture and the aura, suddenly, was weakened.

A spate of midfield injuries affected those matches but Villa’s home form since New Year’s Day includes as many losses as wins in the league – six of each – and failures this season to beat Nottingham Forest (now 17th in the table), Fulham (15th) and Sunderland (19th).

Whatever that indicates about why Villa might be struggling at home, it’s clearly a problem and Emery, while positive about aspects of Villa’s play against the Black Cats, isn’t shying away from that.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

One place where his team don’t come up against the exact challenges posed by some of their Premier League opponents is in the Champions League, where Villa have won two home games out of two in the league phase this season. Indeed, European competitions underpin the very notion of Villa Park as a fortress under Emery, who took Villa back into Europe ahead of the 2023/24 season.

In a recent development, their last home loss in Europe was against Olympiacos in that year’s Conference League semi-finals. They won five out of six at home in the Champions League the next season, drawing the other, and won all seven of their home matches in their successful Europa League campaign in 2025/26.

While the idea of Villa being strong at home has endured, the evidence of it in the Premier League has not.

Sources indicate that villa’s home results in the league might have been short of their expected levels since before the summer, but there are differences between this season and last. Simply selling Morgan Rogers, Ezri Konsa, Emiliano Martinez, Youri Tielemans, Lucas Digne and Ollie Watkins fundamentally changed the picture at Villa Park.

It has been revealed that rogers and Tielemans were vital players for breaking games open. Villa significantly outscored their expected goals value in periods of last season and goals from outside the penalty area were key.

They don’t have the same superpower this season; improving their chance creation is a must and that’s not quick or easy with any group of players, never mind a newly assembled and young team.

While the idea of Villa being strong at home has endured, the evidence of it in the Premier League has not.

It has been revealed that there’s also a looming, inconvenient possibility that’s beginning to sustain the weight of truth. Villa Park is a three-sided stadium this season because the North Stand – ordinarily full of home supporters – is being redeveloped behind one of the goals.

According to recent reports, the difference is intangible, indefinable, but it’s there. Even the players can’t quantify it because half of them have never played at a four-sided Villa Park, but the vacant structure behind the goal makes for an unusual atmosphere.

In a recent development, emery has no interest in excuses. The Villa manager is focused on process and progress, taking every challenge for what it is and finding the answers to the questions they pose.

The North Stand redevelopment won’t be accepted as mitigation for poor home form in the dugout any more than it will in the other three stands, but Emery is no fool. He accepted after the Sunderland draw that Villa Park and the team who call it home are missing ‘something’ without the North Stand. It’s not an excuse, just another test.

Villa need to pass that test. Home results have been a hallmark of the Emery era. The manager himself has qualified for Europe every season since long before he succeeded Steven Gerrard.

It has been revealed that one win in six is a long way short of that standard. Emery’s meticulous and measured problem-solving has been called into action once more.

Industry observers note that the Real Oviedo supporter who racially abused Kylian Mbappé at the Carlos Tartiere has been convicted of a hate crime. The Second Section of the Audiencia Provincial de Asturias delivered the verdict on 17 November 2026. It was a verdict by agreement, known in Spain as conformidad.

The abuse came during Real Oviedo v Real Madrid on 24 August 2025. The fan made monkey gestures and noises in the 37th minute. Real Madrid’s players were celebrating Mbappé’s opening goal at the time.

In a recent development, the man will not go to prison as long as he keeps to the terms of his sentence. The term is suspended on condition that he stays away from football stadiums hosting official competitions for two years, Real Madrid mentioned in an official statement. The prosecuting parties also tied the suspension to a ban from LaLiga stadiums and a ban on approaching Mbappé. The defendant accepted these conditions.

The fine was set at six months at a daily rate of €8. He is also barred from working in education, teaching, sport or leisure for three years and 11 months.

The case was charged under article 510.2.a of the Spanish Criminal Code. LaLiga filed the original complaint. It also supplied expert lip-reading evidence that proved key to resolving the case. Real Madrid later joined the proceedings as a private prosecutor.

The ruling is LaLiga’s twelfth conviction for racism in Spanish football, Servimedia reported. The league presented the outcome as proof of its commitment to fighting racism.

The Carlos Tartiere has featured in this list before. In April 2026, a supporter was convicted over abuse of Marcus Rashford at Real Oviedo v FC Barcelona. That person received a nine-month prison sentence. Another conviction, handed down in September 2025, followed abuse of Iñaki Williams at an Espanyol v Athletic Club match from the 2019/20 season.

According to recent reports, for Real Madrid, the verdict extends a run of cases involving its own players. The club has listed earlier convictions for racist abuse at Mestalla, Son Moix, Vallecas and the José Zorrilla. The Valladolid case ended on 21 May 2025. The Audiencia Provincial de Valladolid convicted five people of hate crimes for abusing Vinícius Júnior at the José Zorrilla on 30 December 2022. Each received a one-year prison sentence.

The pattern points to clubs and the league pursuing racist abuse through the criminal courts rather than leaving it to stadium sanctions alone. In the Oviedo case, the combination of a league complaint and lip-reading evidence was decisive.

Real Madrid is now acting as private prosecutor in other cases involving similar incidents against its players.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in recent years, Louisville City FC have been one of the most successful regular-season teams in United Soccer League history, but it hasn't translated to winning the significant game. They haven't won the USL Championship since 2018, and while this season has been a trying time dealing with injuries and a newly introduced coach taking over, they're playing their best soccer when it matters to set up a strange clash with Sacramento Republic at noon Eastern on Saturday. What's strange isn't that it's Louisville and Sacramento meeting, but that the match kicks off at 9 a.m. local time, a time Louisville forward Ray Serrano states he hasn't played soccer at since he was 15. While it's a regular training time for Louisville and they'll try to keep things on an East Coast timeline, it's hard not to take the shift into account when planning for a final.

It's a challenge that comes with the desire to reach as many fans as possible with a final of this magnitude. Leagues have to work with broadcast networks to ensure that the slots work, and for the USL, having the game on CBS is worth the risk of a 9 a.m. local start with a West Coast team hosting. It's nothing Louisville won't be prepared for, as they look to keep their internal clocks on Eastern Standard Time.

Sources indicate that "No, we're trying to stay on Eastern Time, so for us, it's training time," defender Kyle Adams noted. "Wake up at 8:00 a.m., but really it's 5:00 a.m. Go to sleep a little bit earlier. Try to do everything really just to stay on Eastern Time, eat a little bit earlier on the night before, and just treat it as going into training, and then get after them.".

Other teams have dealt with similar issues, like the Los Angeles Rams when playing an NFL game in Australia, but it's still a struggle to deal with en route to a cup final as Louisville look to reach the pinnacle of the sport for the first time since 2018. Winners of the Prinx Tires USL Cup during the regular season, they do have cup experience that will prove to be fruitful in this competition, which Adams noted has been something that brings the injury-riddled squad together. "We know in the last few years we've struggled in these knockout games, but this year we've turned it on," Serrano mentioned. "It has been really good preparation, just the mentality of going into them, how we deal with the pressure, and we're seeing the fruits of all that now.".

It's cliche to say that because of the adversity that they've dealt with, the club is playing its best soccer when it matters, but between using four goalkeepers during the season and seeing manager Danny Cruz depart to be an assistant manager with Minnesota United, it hasn't been an easy task for interim manager Simon Bird to get this team on the right track at this critical juncture.

According to recent reports, "Going back to the main part is the adversity that we've faced. You mentioned injuries, having to deal with that side of it, some of the various parts of the season, different things we've had to deal with from a tactical or technical standpoint, where we've lost games, and we feel that we shouldn't have lost games," Bird said when reflecting on the team's development under his leadership. "The most impressive thing I said to the guys today, yesterday in training, we worked on our defensive structure, but the whole training session I thought was excellent, not just the defensive side, off the ball but with the ball, and to see it all come together towards the end of the season is really rewarding. Hopefully, we can carry that on and put together a complete performance, and that's what we've had throughout the season-moments where we've let ourselves down in all these different areas, set pieces, maybe transition at other times, in front of goal. So, putting it all together for a complete performance on Saturday is the goal.".

It has been revealed that traveling away to a tough environment in Heart Health Park, Louisville will meet the hottest team in the league in Sacramento Republic. They've ridden a club-record 16-game unbeaten run to the final based on their defense. That has set a strong foundation to build on, and it could make the final one where the first team to score a goal wins the match. Sacramento's squad also has experience in USL Cup finals, which goes a long way when preparing for games of this stature.

In a recent development, "I don't think it can hurt to have that. This would be a step forward for my first final. I think experience is invaluable for players and for staff," Sacramento coach Neil Collins said. "But then there's also the recognition that every game is different, every team is different, and every season is different. So it's just trying to get the balance right and enjoy the opportunity. You've got to have the mechanisms to control the things you can control. Obviously, the opposition team is trying to do the same, and we've got to do everything we can to be ready to take the opportunity when it comes. But the experience will definitely help us; there's plenty of that in our dressing room.".

It's a final where the best that the league has to offer will be on display, and it couldn't come at a better time. The summer of soccer, with the United States hosting the World Cup alongside Mexico and Canada, has truly turned into a soccer avalanche, and this final showcases one of the top atmospheres in the league. You can't ask for much better than that, as no matter what, a drought will come to an end. Sacramento Republic haven't won the final since 2014, while Louisville haven't won since 2018, and for these clubs, it will mean a lot to get back to the top.

  • La Dea needed to get back on their feet, as after beating Pafos in the opener, they lost to Ajax and were held 1-1 by Kairat Almaty.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Atalanta wasted so many chances in Bosnia, but after Borac went down to nine men, completed another incredible comeback to win 3-2 with Nikola Krstovic, Sead Kolasinac and Davide Zappacosta.

La Dea needed to get back on their feet, as after beating Pafos in the opener, they lost to Ajax and were held 1-1 by Kairat Almaty. Marco Carnesecchi joined Isak Hien, Odilon Kossounou and Thomas Pompei on the absentee list, so Marco Sportiello took the gloves. FK Borac had one win and two defeats in the Conference League, but Srdan Grahovac and Stefan Savic were injured.

See how it all unfolded on the Liveblog.

Giacomo Raspadori’s low drive forced a tricky save in the first three minutes, while Lorenzo Bernasconi did just enough to prevent Luka Juricic getting on the end of a cross from the left.

Raspadori turned his angled drive across the face of goal after Jonathan Rowe won the ball back in midfield, but Juricic failed to make the most of a Mario Pasalic failed defensive header.

Atalanta continued to waste chances, Pasalic this time skimming the upright from a tight angle, then Raspadori too slow to get on the end of an Ederson roll across.

They were made to pay for it, as Borac took the lead when a low cross from the left was flicked on by Omar Sijaric for Juricic, who was able to control with his back to goal, turn Sead Kolasinac and sweep in from eight yards.

Just as La Dea were pushing forward, they were caught out on the counter again down the same flank, this time the Juricic cross was flicked in at the near post by Matej Deket.

Raspadori’s effort inside the area was charged down by Branimir Cipetic, while the goalkeeper got a glove to the Nicola Zalewski cross-shot and Pasalic was unable to turn in the rebound after the restart.

Industry observers note that atalanta’s finishing remained a huge problem, as Pasalic was sent through by Rowe only to blast over from seven yards. Incredibly, when Mladen Jurkas was off his line after misplacing the pass out from a corner, Rowe still managed to fire wide of the open goal.

David Vukovic threatened a third for Borac, his volley going wide from the edge of the D on a cleared corner, and the Sandi Ogrinec header clipped the top of the crossbar on 67 minutes.

Charles De Ketelaere was almost as bad with his finishing, somehow turning over from close range on the rebound from the save on Pasalic.

Recent findings suggest that borac went down to 10 men after Abel Pascual hauled down Rowe just outside the area for an inevitable red card. On the resulting free kick, Rowe found himself clear on goal at the near post, but fired straight at the goalkeeper’s face from point-blank range.

Davide Zappacosta saw a scorcher deflected over for a corner, and Atalanta finally got one back when Raoul Bellanova floated a cross to the back post for the Krstovic header.

Moments later, Borac went down to nine men, as Sebastijan Herrera received a straight red card for his wild tackle from behind on Zalewski.

On the resulting Zalewski free kick, it was deflected onto the upright by a Borac defender, but Sead Kolasinac was ready to bundle the rebound over the line and draw 2-2.

Just days after coming back from 4-2 down to hold Inter 4-2 in Serie A, Atalanta did it again by completing the turnaround from 2-0 down to win 3-2 in Bosnia. Davide Zappacosta cut inside from the left and blasted right-footed into the far bottom corner in added time.

Juricic 22 (B), Deket 30 (B), Krstovic 86 (A), Kolasinac 90 (A), Zappacosta 93 (A).

HENRY WINTER: Bruno Fernandes has been a brilliant servant, but it's time to cut the cord at Manchester United

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Manchester United are under newly introduced management and need to be under new leadership on the field.
  • Industry observers note that bruno Fernandes has undeniably been a flickering beacon of brief hope for United in darkening times.
  • It has been revealed that even taking up the year’s option (unless to increase the player’s transfer fee) would be a retrograde step.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester United are under newly introduced management and need to be under new leadership on the field.

Industry observers note that bruno Fernandes has undeniably been a flickering beacon of brief hope for United in darkening times. He’s been their Player of the Year in five of the last seven seasons, risen to 19th of their greatest scorers with 113 goals, has scored 75 times (24 pens, four free-kicks) and provided 74 assists in 240 Premier League games and is the reigning Footballer of the Year. But it’s undeniably time for the club to face reality, resist the urge to extend a contract which expires next summer and build for the future.

It has been revealed that even taking up the year’s option (unless to increase the player’s transfer fee) would be a retrograde step. Fernandes is 32, slowing up, and not now “best in class, 10 out of 10s” to borrow Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s catchphrase. He is not the most convincing of captains, moans too much and flaps his arms like a fledgling dove attempting to leave the nest.

Fernandes would never, ever be considered one of United’s elite captains in a strong, historic field that includes Sir Bobby Charlton, Roy Keane, Bryan Robson, Steve Bruce, Roger Byrne, Nemanja Vidic and Gary Neville, amongst others.

All are different; Neville was very vocal, Charlton led by example, but were united in their total commitment.

In a recent development, fernandes’ leadership qualities were brought into question when he openly criticised the tactics of Michael Carrick, effectively undermining him. That may not have been Fernandes’ intention when questioning the tactical approach against Como but it certainly didn’t help Carrick at a time when he needed players standing up to be counted, not standing up to his tactics in public. Such concerns – some of them legitimate – should have been aired in private.

According to recent reports, it indicated a lack of leadership from Fernandes, a lack of gratitude, too. Fernandes wouldn’t have been named the writers’ Footballer of the Year and the players’ Player of the Year without Carrick reviving United’s fortunes and their No. 8’s form last season.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

In receiving the writers’ award in May, Fernandes eulogised about the interim head coach, praising “the amazing job” he did in guiding United into the Champions League and saying Carrick possesses the “great character to become a top manager”.

Such an endorsement from such an influential figure at the club, effectively the voice of the dressing-room, undoubtedly contributed to Ineos and the Glazers appointing Carrick to the permanent role.

Industry observers note that bruno’s voice is powerful. That is why it was damaging when he spoke out against Carrick’s tactics. “Lies,” was Bruno’s reaction to some of the interpretation of his words but mud stuck.

Sources indicate that carrick questioned individuals’ running stats – without naming Fernandes – and then dropped him for the game against Bournemouth. United need real leaders. In fairness to Fernandes, there are plenty of stories of the good work he does behind the scenes.

Who would inherit the armband in the unlikely event that Carrick’s successor, Mauricio Pochettino, was brave and looked to the future? Matthijs de Ligt, an Ajax captain at 18, would be a strong contender were it not for his back problems. Senne Lammens represents United admirably on and off the field, and was one of only two who emerged with reputation intact from Anfield.

According to recent reports, the other was Kobbie Mainoo. It might seem a leap of faith in one so young, still only 21, but Mainoo could perform the duties until a more experienced leader was recruited by the club that once bought Keane, Bruce, Vidic etc. (All of this is a reminder of United’s need to buy leaders, powerful characters as well as good players).

Mainoo’s one of the few deserving of his place at the moment. He’s also an academy graduate, a local lad, and a link to great home-grown generations. Fans would love that re-affirmation of United’s identity. It would be quite a statement by Pochettino.

It has been revealed that mainoo has only minimal captaincy experience against Bayern Munich in 2017 (as a kid) and successfully with England Under-19s in 2023. More recently, more pertinently, Mainoo acted like a leader against Roma on November 3 when others were losing their discipline.

Industry observers note that it’s still too early, of course, and Mainoo is still developing but he could do the honours on a temporary basis in the unlikely event that United cut the cord with Fernandes. But a recruitment department incapable of making strong decisions and buying “best in class” – they were not in the running when Elliot Anderson and Morgan Rogers were available in the summer - may be tempted to go for the easy option of keeping Fernandes, rather than step into a new era.

Henry Winter is one of football's most popular and respected writers. Previously the Chief Football Writer for The Times and a Football Correspondent for The Daily Telegraph, his work now primarily features on his Substack. He has also lauched his own podcast 'The Winter View'.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that an Amazon Prime documentary series about the Glazers' Tampa Bay Buccaneers American football team paints a revealing picture of the billionaire family coalescing around a sport they actually love.
  • All six children of Malcolm Glazer, the man who built the business empire and bought United in 2005, share stories of their childhood NFL obsession.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By IAN HERBERT - DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER.

Published: 12:00 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 12:03 EST, 24 November 2026.

It has been revealed that an Amazon Prime documentary series about the Glazers' Tampa Bay Buccaneers American football team paints a revealing picture of the billionaire family coalescing around a sport they actually love. It feels a very long way from Manchester United, the club they have taken down to the depths.

All six children of Malcolm Glazer, the man who built the business empire and bought United in 2005, share stories of their childhood NFL obsession. Darcie Glazer Kassewitz, sister to five Glazer brothers, relates how, on the day before they all went to a Miami Dolphins game, her brothers would be in the basement with bedsheets and paint creating huge banners.

In a recent development, sometimes playing ‘knee football’ down there. Or competing in what they called the ‘BYFL’ – the ‘back-yard football league’ they set up among themselves and neighbours. ‘They all loved sports,’ says their mother, Linda.

Of course, the British form of football doesn’t feature.

This homespun scene contrasts with the family’s current dismay about the chaos created at Manchester United, which has led to renewed discussion among several of the siblings about selling off some, or all, of their shareholding.

Most of the siblings consider selling a minority share to Sir Jim Ratcliffe to have been a mistake, according to a source with a social connection to the Glazers. Though there is not a sense of how the family feel about individual Ratcliffe appointees, they are thought to rue the departure of Richard Arnold – former United commercial director and chief executive, whose part working on dozens of commercial deals saw him oversee around £4billion of revenue.

Manchester United's dismal form this season hasn't gone unnoticed by their owners in the United States, some of whom have discussed cashing in on their shareholding.

Industry observers note that american football - and their team the Tampa Bay Buccaneers - is the Glazers' true love. Joel Glazer led the celebrations when they won the Super Bowl in 2021.

The Glazers have been ‘surprised’ at the loss of other influential senior staff, according to the source.

Sources indicate that arnold saw the writing on the wall before Ratcliffe and Ineos arrived. He personally negotiated his own exit with the Glazers. But they were then unable to prevent other departures which have been detrimental to the club, according to sources with no Glazer connection who have worked with United.

Those lost include the highly respected Victoria Timpson, United's former 'CEO of Alliances and Partnerships', who struck the Snapdragon and Teamviewer shirt sponsorship deal, but left in December 2024.

Florence Lafaye, former United commercial director, briefly took over Timpson’s responsibilities but also left to join Timpson in establishing the commercial agency Altius8, which was soon hired by Tottenham Hotspur.

Joel, Avram and Bryan Glazer are the three siblings thought to relish owning United – a calling card they have used at, among other settings, the Davos World Economic Forum, where United were the only football club to take a pavilion in the past.

Joel, whose 10.7 per cent shareholding is the biggest of the six siblings, was often seen as a man of interference before Ratcliffe’s arrival, pushing for higher fees when executive vice chairman Ed Woodward or others were trying to negotiate a transfer sale.

But the interest in United of Kevin, Ed and Darcie is far less certain, even though all six sit on the United board and Darcie holds the second largest share at 9.71 per cent.

It has been revealed that the six collectively wanted to test the water for a sale after seeing US financier Todd Boehly pay £4.25billion for Chelsea in 2022. They formed the impression that United could sell for twice that much.

The sale of a share to Ratcliffe was held up by the six failing to agree on whether to sell up entirely or just let go of the football side of the business.

Most of the Glazer siblings consider selling a minority share of Manchester United to Sir Jim Ratcliffe to have been a mistake.

The interest in Manchester United of Kevin, Ed and Darcie Glazer (pictured) is far from certain, even though all six sit on the United board.

An extensive report about United by Bloomberg last week suggested some individual family members were considering the sale of more of their shareholding and hoping to convince others among the six to join them.

In a recent development, the unexpected summer purchase of a stake in Liverpool by a Jeff Bezos-led consortium had caught several members of the family ‘off guard’, leaving some of the six feeling they had missed an opportunity to cash out. That deal has a potential takeover clause which could value Liverpool at £5.3bn.

The original proposal was that Ratcliffe would ultimately buy the rest of United for £4bn, but since buying into the club, his chemicals business has been hit by a prolonged industrial downturn, collapsing profitability and high energy costs.

The Ineos Industries division recorded a £1.84bn pre-tax loss in 2025, his chemicals empire is carrying more than £10bn of net debt and he has been exiting from most of his sports interests.

The Glazers have the power, under the terms of their deal with Ratcliffe, to sell the club outright and force him to sell his stake. Another option would be to divest themselves of a small slice of their 48.9 per cent stake. But the current uncertainty about the future landscape of the Premier League created by the Manchester City case, with a slew of possible legal cases in its wake, is impacting on outside investment in top-flight clubs.

The family may have to sit tight and hope the recovery of the club’s fortunes, allied to intends for a latest £2bn stadium, will take the club’s value closer to the £6bn that the six would be likely to agree on as an exit figure. They could tap into the bond market as Barcelona did to finance their $1.5bn upgrade of Camp Nou, or look to private equity funds, who would want a major pay-back when the stadium is built.

But for the first time through their 21 years as owners, United face the frightening predicament of relegation – bringing, for example, a £5.7million-a-year TV deal in the Championship compared with the £191.5m in Premier League income banked last season.

With upcoming Premier League Squad Cost Ratio rules allowing the club to spend 85 per cent of last year’s £677.6m revenue on players and £160m in the club’s rotating credit facility, there is money.

Multiple sources say the Glazers stepped in to ensure Mauricio Pochettino’s appointment – something United deny.

The Glazer family are thought to rue the departure of Richard Arnold (pictured), the club's former commercial director and chief executive.

In a recent development, multiple sources say the Glazers stepped in to ensure Mauricio Pochettino’s appointment – something United deny. But the source close to the family also believes they will now continue to present a greater challenge to what many see as Ratcliffe’s running down of the United operation.

The Bloomberg report highlighted how Ratcliffe’s 300 job cuts had focused heavily on commercial, media and administrative divisions, which former employees said had eroded relations with corporate partners and caused a deterioration in the level of service.

Industry observers note that A former executive described how long-standing sponsors, accustomed to receiving complimentary autographed merchandise, were told they should expect to pay shipping fees for signed memorabilia. ‘Penny wise, pound foolish,’ the executive stated. This was certainly not the Glazer way under Woodward and Arnold, who built that side of the operation.

The Glazers are 47th in the Forbes list of most wealthy US families and the Amazon Tampa Bay Bucs series reveals an innate obsession with the financial bottom line and making profit. ‘My father didn’t give a damn about what anybody else thought,’ Ed Glazer tells the film-makers. ‘He would always say, “Why can’t we do this?”. We could look at anything as long as the numbers made sense.’.

It’s hard to believe that Ratcliffe, a man desperately trying to preserve his own business, is going to get in the way of the Glazers seeking ways to preserve the long-neglected asset which is now staring into the abyss.
